That depends greatly on the particular game, the libraries it uses, and any of dozens of other factors.

However, in general, the more closely "related" two distros are in terms of space and time, the more readily you can get the software to work with minimal hassle. I've had .deb packages I've ganked from one Debian-based distro and run it on another with no problems. Basing on Debian is a pretty sound move.

Really there's only a few options here.

  1. Put it out on .deb - works, often will have cross-distro portability. If they test it against Ubuntu, Mint, and a few other Debian-based distros (Knoppix comes to mind, although it's more of a super Live CD), they're probably good, and can pretty easily make slightly modified versions for a number of them.

  2. Put it on .rpm - same as .deb, but the cross-compatibility won't be there. EDIT: I should word this better. The cross-compatibility with Debian-based distros will, not surprisingly, not be there. Also, while RPM does work between distros, in my experience it is a lot more finicky than Debian. At the very least it should be tested against Fedora (which implies compatibility with Red Hat Linux itself) and SuSE, which is AFAIK the most popular distro that uses it without being directly affiliated with Red Hat. Plus, RPM is based on Red Hat (which is ultimately Fedora), and that tends to be more business-oriented these days.

  3. Stand-alone binary package - This is actually how a lot of commercial programs used to come for Linux. Works in that it's distro-independent, doesn't work in that it can break surprisingly readily, and also has varying degrees of success in terms of dynamic libraries (which can result in huge binaries with critical breakage points if you have to resort to static linking).

  4. Source - The best and worst compatibility option. Best because it will work on quite literally almost any distribution, including Linux From Scratch (an actual distro based on teaching you to build your own Linux system from a pile of source packages) and Gentoo (a system designed around recompiling almost every package on the computer for maximum optimization). Worst because an ordinary user is going to smash their head through the monitor trying to figure out WTF happens when one of the dozens of libraries it runs on isn't installed, there's a conflict between two header files somewhere, or a GCC bug decides to throw up all over things. This is surprisingly common in a lot of cases. It can make even people who are used to programming give up on a program, since most of the time they don't have the time, inclination or expertise to hunt down the problem and fix it, particularly if it's pervasive throughout the program. As a very rough example that has workarounds but illustrates the point, at least if you have any familiarity with C or C++, a program written to produce a 32-bit binary, but you need to compile it in 64-bits, therefore resulting in a program constantly miscalculating the size of the data it's trying to move around, which gets really nasty really fast. Also, there's the whole thing about a lot of companies trying to keep their source closed, which makes this nonviable for a lot of them, philosophical open source considerations completely aside.

So you can support any combination of these options with varying degrees of success and/or failure. As a general rule of thumb, the more things your program depends on that you can't bring along with you, the more that can and will go wrong. As another general rule of thumb, the package management system will at least TRY to keep things consistent enough so that you're reasonably sure that if you successfully install the package you can run it, and if your program needs something else it will try to get it or inform the user as to what it needs.

Unfortunately IMNSHO cross-distro compatibility and software installation is one of the rockiest parts of Linux, and I suspect that it's a not-often-talked-about source of a lot of the problems that you see cropping up that non-technical users complain about after they've worked with it for a while and suddenly their previously fantastic Linux system starts borking itself up.
